source_en: Delivering textiles to the market.
Two bolts of wool sold. Good day!
Home to my room above Samuil's teahouse.
Medical supplies for the triage center.
Traded my last silk for bandages.
Selling batteries. Fair prices, as always!
Home above the teahouse before curfew.
Walking the ash roads. Bazaar is empty.
Mandatory merchant residency count.
Home from eight hours at the steel mill.
Visiting grandmother. I have no children.
Going home. Travel makes me ill.
Gave up trading. The road is hopeless.
Getting my first passport. Never left Georgia.
Hauling timber for the sawmill, as usual.
Packing for my first trip ever.
Pension, after forty years at the tractor plant.
Going home to wait for the end. No hope.
Merhaba, officer! A fine day to guard such an important gate, no?
My ID lives beside my lucky chestnut. It never fails me!
I took a shortcut through the mist and met a very polite cow.
I spilled a little tea on the form. The information survived!
I found a door in the ruins today. It smelled of cinnamon.
The world is putting on pajamas, officer. A very long nap.
May your tea be hot and your path clear!
You have a kind face. Don't let the gray change it.
Until we meet in a brighter chapter. Stay well!
My grandmother said small rooms have the best conversations.
Once I waited three days in customs. This is easy!
The longest journey… ends the same… as the short ones…
Tell my son… his father… had a fine long trip…
Where are you coming from?
The market! Two bolts of wool, then Samuil's black tea. Good day.
The triage center. My last silk for bandages and batteries. Fair deal.
The ash roads. The bazaar is empty, so I walk and see what stands.
The tram depot! Twenty years driving the number four. Never missed a stop.
My flat. I live alone. Nobody to trip over, nobody to feed.
The border! I arrived this morning. My first time in your town!
Are you experiencing any symptoms?
Only my knees. Thirty years of roads. They complain, I ignore them.
A dusty cough. And I lose my chestnut daily. It always returns.
My heart flutters sometimes. I sit, drink tea if there is tea.
My knees? Perfect. Thirty years at an office desk, barely walking.
No cough. I have not left the house in a month.
Healthy as a bull. And tea? Never touch it. Never liked it.
Want to hold my lucky chestnut? It helps, truly.
In the bazaar we say a cloudy sky is better shade for merchants.
My boots squeak today. A joke, I think. I lack the punchline.
Don't mind my humming. An old song to shorten the road.
Don't be sad, officer. Next story, maybe I hold the stamp.
My father survived three disasters. After each, he said: have some tea.
